items.title: "We Dodged A Bomb": Ex-Con Trainee Indicted Over Device That Emptied 2,500 Homes Around Illinois Ethanol Plant
items.content_text:
"We Dodged A Bomb": Ex-Con Trainee Indicted Over Device That Emptied 2,500 Homes Around Illinois Ethanol Plant

A federal grand jury has indicted a 41-year-old trainee at the Peoria, Illinois, ethanol plant where a bomb was found last Friday, charging him with emailing the company a threat that explosive devices had been placed there. Andrew Kozak of Chillicothe pleaded not guilty to both counts on Tuesday.

The threat reached BioUrja Renewables on Friday, Nov. 13, and police found a package at the plant that afternoon. Bomb technicians had it rendered safe by 9:12 p.m., and Police Chief Brad Dixon stressed that it was not a hoax. Peoria police ordered everyone within a mile of the plant to evacuate, including parts of downtown Peoria and East Peoria. Dixon said the order displaced people from an estimated 2,500 homes, and it stayed in place for 18 hours. The FBI has since taken over the case and confirmed the device was a real explosive.

The indictment charges Kozak with threats regarding explosives, for threatening to damage and destroy the plant by fire and an explosive, and with interstate communication of a threat. U.S. Attorney Gregory Gilmore said Kozak emailed BioUrja that a bomb would be detonated, and called the threat credible. The first count carries up to 10 years in federal prison and the second up to five.

🚨#INDICTMENT: A grand jury returned an indictment charging Andrew M. Kozak with one count of transmitting via interstate or foreign commerce a threat to unlawfully damage and destroy the BioUrga Renewables plant in Peoria, Illinois, by means of fire and an explosive, and one... pic.twitter.com/81m6IZ7HTx

— FBI Springfield (@FBISpringfield) November 17, 2026

"While law enforcement regularly responds to bomb threats, most are deemed not credible," Ryan Presley, the special agent in charge of the FBI's Springfield office, said at Tuesday's press conference announcing the charges. "But in this instance, it was. Had it not been for the swift action of the responders and the bomb technicians, this incident could have had a very different outcome."

ICYMI: #FBISpringfield Special Agent in Charge Ryan Presley thanked law enforcement partners and the community at the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of Illinois' press conference announcing the indictment of Andrew M. Kozak following the identification of an... pic.twitter.com/U3wGqHyHxL

— FBI Springfield (@FBISpringfield) November 17, 2026

Neither count accuses Kozak of planting the device, and officials declined to say who built or planted it, how many devices there were or how powerful the one found was. The criminal complaint is sealed. Federal sources told NBC Chicago that investigators believe Kozak left the bomb at the plant and then sent the threat, and that he showed up for work on Monday morning to avoid drawing suspicion. He was arrested when he arrived.

FBI agents served a search warrant at Kozak's home in Chillicothe, about 15 miles north of Peoria, and ATF agents were seen carrying out evidence bags, NewsChannel 20 reported.

Kozak had worked at the plant as a trainee for about 10 months, according to his LinkedIn page, where he described the job as "Learning how to operate an ethanol plant."

State records reviewed by Fox News show Kozak served two stints in Nebraska state prison for burglary, paroled in 2008 and again in 2014, with burglary-related felony convictions in four counties. NBC Chicago found that two of those burglaries were at public high schools in Polk County.

At his initial appearance, Kozak told the court his middle initial is K, not the M on the indictment, Capitol City Now reported. Judge Ronald Hanna appointed federal public defender Jessica Douglas to represent him.

"We didn't dodge a bullet. We dodged a bomb," Peoria Mayor Rita Ali said. The plant can produce 135 million gallons of ethanol a year, and the evacuation canceled events across downtown Peoria, including at the Peoria Civic Center.

Prosecutors want Kozak held until trial, and he stays in U.S. Marshals custody until a detention hearing at 11 a.m. on Friday. A pre-trial conference is set for Dec. 3, and a jury trial for Jan. 11.

items.title: Anthropic's Founders Slipped A Chilling Warning Into Their IPO Letter
items.content_text:
Anthropic's Founders Slipped A Chilling Warning Into Their IPO Letter

The founders' letter at the beginning of Anthropic's IPO prospectus carries a warning about what the company's own product could do in the wrong hands: "Authoritarian governments may use AI to create high-tech surveillance states, deepen repression, and make themselves much more difficult to dislodge."

The letter, signed by all seven co-founders including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, names "authoritarian abuse" as one of four broad categories of AI risk, alongside misuse, loss of control and economic disruption. Its answer to the surveillance threat is a single sentence: Anthropic is "committed to working with free societies to provide a counterweight to authoritarian abuse and to promote freedom and democracy."

One page earlier, Anthropic discloses that they sell AI to governments as a way to "build technological state capacity." "We already work with the U.S. federal government, many state governments, and U.S. allies in areas such as child services, social security administration, cybersecurity, and intelligence collection," the founders wrote.

The prospectus also spells out where Anthropic draws the line. Its usage policy bars the use of its models for fully autonomous weapons or "mass surveillance, including mass domestic surveillance," and the company says holding that line has cost it revenue. After Anthropic took that position publicly in February, President Trump directed federal agencies to stop using its technology and the Pentagon designated it a "supply-chain risk to national security." According to the filing, the Department of War also suggested it could invoke the Defense Production Act to force Anthropic to drop the limits.

Alex Randall, a researcher at the Center for Humane Technology and a former policy adviser to Britain's Cabinet Office and Ministry of Defence, argues in UnHerd that the letter "moves on, leaving this statement unexplained," and that the risk it names is not confined to foreign dictatorships.

For most of history, Randall writes, surveillance was capped by the number of people a state could pay to read what it collected: East Germany's Stasi kept files on a third of the population and never had enough officers to read them. The transformer, the 2017 architecture behind Claude, ChatGPT and their rivals, removed that cap. Its "attention" mechanism weighs every input against every other, and multi-modal models can fuse location, video, audio, financial records and browsing habits into a single framework. "We have now built more officers than will ever be needed," Randall writes.

Under consumer terms Anthropic announced in August 2025, users of Claude's Free, Pro and Max plans decide whether their chats can be used to train its models, and Anthropic keeps the data of those who say yes for five years. TechCrunch noted at the time that the training toggle in the pop-up shown to existing users was set to "On" by default. Business, government, education and API customers are excluded.

Randall's point is that every exchange with a chatbot, Claude or any other, reveals preferences and vulnerabilities, and each one feeds a loop that gets better at predicting what the user wants, thinks and will do next.

In 2021 the Defense Intelligence Agency told Sen. Ron Wyden in a memo that its analysts had searched commercially bought smartphone location data on Americans without a warrant, in five investigations over two and a half years. In January, defense contractor Reveal Technology acquired Anomaly Six, whose tools "map global digital activity" and analyze behavior. Randall traces the ambition back a quarter century, to Adm. John Poindexter's DARPA program to track terrorists by correlating existing data streams, and argues that "total information awareness" is now becoming the default outcome of the AI race.

His conclusion is bleak: if the sensor web keeps expanding and is wired into ever more capable AI, whoever's AI it is, it will soon be trivial to know what any person or group wants and intends, and whoever controls the machines will be able to see revolutions coming long before they form.

Anthropic's latest amended filing, dated Nov. 17, sets the offering at 825 million Class A shares, at an assumed $74 each, the midpoint of its range. The founders' letter closes by telling buyers that everyone who owns the stock, "whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort" to steer the technology.

items.title: Anti-Realpolitik Economics?
items.content_text:
Anti-Realpolitik Economics?

By Michael Every of Rabobank

Another day, another IT system down – now the classified US intelligence communications network; oh, and the CIA building was on fire.

Assuming this is IT and not CYA related, note Huang is not going to return as Nvidia CEO and the SEC Is probing the giant firm, which despite doubling its revenue says it will be “selective” about who it backstops in the AI ecosystem. To say that there could be a price for not being in the winners’ circle (or “circular financing”, as some put it) is an understatement. 

In markets, the Financial Times reports Paris and Berlin have sealed the ECB succession for Spain’s de Cos; that’s as the Fed’s Cook is refusing to attend a hearing convened by President Trump; and as Brazil’s central bank official has warned that stablecoin transfers may constitute money laundering,which depends on the transaction, but is also a possible (geo)political stance given the US dominance in that arena.

In geopolitics, Iran rejected reports it’s planning a dirty-bomb attack. The US struck Qeshm again following an Iranian attack on a US base in Bahrain, followed by Iranian drones swarming Kuwait. The New York Times just flagged that Iran’s dams may hide and power missile bases, making them potential military targets; Iran then stated all infrastructure close to anything military in the GCC, Israel, and states helping attack it will be targets if war restarts. Elsewhere, Iraq’s pro-Iran Kataib Hezbollah militia refused to withdraw from its stronghold near Baghdad ahead of Friday’s deadline, and the Houthis advanced again inside Yemen.

Ukraine successfully destroyed a section of the key Russian Crimea bridge. Russia is plotting its response, and the US scolded Kyiv over its deep strikes ahead of fresh peace talks, seeing push-back from Germany. 

Trump kicked off his Asia trip by joining his first Quad summit leaders’ meeting for two years: the group expressed “grave concerns” about economic coercion and announced a new maritime security initiative and military drills. That was as two Russian military jets buzzed close to Taiwan, the Philippines and South Korea announced defence and infrastructure cooperation, and Thailand opened its markets to the US and pledged to purchase more agri goods even as it is a target of the US crackdown on AI chip exports that will impact its datacentre plans. 

In geoeconomics, Trump claimed the US will have enough rare earths in 10 months(!) That follows last week’s San Francisco Declaration on the Secure Foundations of Enduring Prosperity between the US, Australia, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea, Qatar, Singapore, the UAE, and the UK; they have pledged to coordinate against “economic coercion, supply chain disruptions, and non-market policies and practices,” --the latter rhymes with China-- to protect “sensitive technologies and critical infrastructure from undue access, influence, or control.”

Canada’s PM Carney spoke of deeper cooperation with China: in exchange for more EVs and steel imports for two years, Beijing will reopen the market for pork and seafood exports. Yet those EVs replace higher value-added local auto production already threatened by US tariffs and the steel is a specific security issue for the US. As the Canadian press puts it, ‘Carney secures another China trade deal - but at what cost?’ as “China hawks urge PM to be wary of country he once called the 'biggest security threat'”; and ‘If Carney tries to play China against the US, Canada will lose’ as “Beijing is no replacement for Washington.”

UK PM Burnham delayed his options for a closer relationship with the EU until December despite the EU-UK summit on Friday. He’s now planning to release it alongside his ‘10-year plan’, which is logical: but so is having a clear idea about defence spending, which won’t happen until next year, while the long-awaited Milburn welfare reform report out yesterday is already seen to face political challenges despite not slashing state spending. 

Over the Channel, Marine Le Pen floated lowering France’s retirement age to as low as 60. Let’s see how the electoral then the fiscal maths math on that front – and recall the main presidential challenger from the left is calling for de facto default on some French government debt, showing most French voters, for now, favour populism of one form or another.

That’s as the economist Isabelle Weber is plugging her new book on, ‘Anti-Fascist Economics’, which argues for establishing: 

‘A floor for livelihoods’, where the state guarantees that essential goods and services remain universally affordable and accessible via nationalisation, price controls, strategic stockpiling, and redundant capacity; and

‘A ceiling on wealth concentration’ with limits on wealth accumulation, corporate monopolies, and profiteering in critical sectors via anti-trust actions and taxation. Indeed, Weber argues against trade wars or protectionism and for international cooperation to stabilise global supply chains, food security, and green transitions. 

Her ideas run parallel to MMT (Modern Monetary Theory) in implying other countries will agree to supply goods and services to an ‘anti-fascist economy’ state, even if it runs inflationary monetized fiscal deficits. The US is the only economy who can get away with that until now due to the Eurodollar, and even that position is seen as challenged by US deindustrialisation and the resulting potential loss of global military primacy in places like the Middle East. (Recall my longstanding use of the term ‘Post-Post-Keynesian’.)

Weber’s arguments seem to appeal to many looking at opinion polls and election results. However, will the current winning demographics and institutions in all countries, and trade surplus countries with massive militaries, agree to rebalance their economies? History isn’t full of peace and harmony, sadly – will the APEC summit be? If not, Weber may be offering ‘Anti-Realpolitik Economics’ absent a global swing to the new ideological “-ism” she seems to define as ‘post-national socialism’.

The only alternative to the status quo is then if some countries or blocs follow her ideas via neomercantilism --a trade surplus exchange-rate ‘firewall’ allowing for fiscal expansion while commodity supply chains are kept under control to keep prices reasonable-- and capital controls. Yet doesn’t it look like the nationalist, corporatist economics that some academics define as ‘fascist’ if only some do it? 

While this may all sound too meta to many market participants, it’s the often-unrecognised core issue behind most of what we see unfolding around us, as states and stakeholders push for either continuity of the old system Weber rails against or new, clashing alternatives to it. Re-read the news in this Daily again with the above in mind and see if you join any dots differently.

items.title: WTI Extends Losses After Big Crude Build, Record Production; Shrugs Off Tanker Attacks
items.content_text:
WTI Extends Losses After Big Crude Build, Record Production; Shrugs Off Tanker Attacks

Oil prices are tumbling for no good reason (oddly triggered simultaneously across many asset-classes at the US equity cash open), erasing morning gains driven by yet more tankers coming under attack in the MidEast and refineries wrecked in Russia. As we discuss at the end of this note, it appears traders are eying a new regime in crude trading.

"Further disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz remain an important upside risk, but rising OPEC+ output, resilient Russian exports and building U.S. inventories point to a more comfortable supply picture," analysts at ING say. 

"We continue to expect the oil balance to loosen as supply recovers, limiting the scope for a sustained rebound in prices."

Oil prices had slipped lower yesterday evening on the back of sizable builds reported by API, now to see if the official data backs that up...

API

  • Crude +5.3mm
  • Cushing -1.7mm
  • Gasoline +5.1mm
  • Distillates +351k

DOE

  • Crude +3.38mm (+2.7mm exp)
  • Cushing -1.209mm
  • Gasoline +5.192mm - biggest build since Jan
  • Distillates +1.571mm

While not as large as API, the official data did confirm a second weekly build in crude stocks and a very large rise in gasoline inventories (biggest since January) as Cushing drew back down towards 'tank bottoms'...

The SPR saw another large draw (3.174mm barrels - the most since August)...

...leaving the SPR just 6mm barrels from record lows...

Despite the big build, total US Distillates stocks remain at record lows for this time of year...

US Crude production rose to a new record high as the rig county continues to climb...

WTI was hovering around $83 ahead of the official print and extended losses after the big build and production jump...

So where does that leave us? 

The past two sessions sum up the new regime. Brent lost over 3% on Monday as signs of recovery in the flow of oil in the Strait of Hormuz increased expectations of a supply surplus. That happened even though Iran attacked a US base in Bahrain and claimed more Hormuz mine strikes. A year ago, that headline alone would have put $5 on the barrel. 

Now the market is looking past the explosions to the balances, and those have turned. The IEA now sees supply exceeding demand by 1.7 million barrels per day in Q4, and observed global inventories rose 52 million barrels, the first monthly increase since June. Last night’s API added to it, with U.S. crude stocks up 5.3 million barrels in the week ending Nov 13, after a 9 million barrel build the week before. 

The less discussed half of the story is demand. Consumption destroyed at $130 crude isn’t coming back just because Brent is in the low $90s. The IEA sees world oil demand falling by 2.7 mb/d in 2026, to 102.3 mb/d, and even next year’s rebound is mostly petrochemicals, while high prices, electrification and fuel efficiency in the global vehicle fleet dampen the rebound in road fuels demand. 

In other words, the war pulled forward some structural demand loss that won’t come back. That said, the bears may be getting ahead of themselves on supply. Dated Brent is still $22/bbl above pre-war levels. Iraq is trucking oil via Syria, which suggests its flows are not yet back to pre-war levels, and LSEG warns that normalization of Hormuz flows “is still not possible under current conditions.” 

With Brent down 21% this month and shorts piling in, one confirmed tanker loss in the Strait could cause a short squeeze much bigger than the fundamentals justify. Demand is the slow, structural force here and supply is the fast, headline-driven one. For now the market is betting on demand, but bets on Hormuz have been wrong before.

Small Vessel Trade Thrives in Hormuz As Iran Targets Supertankers

By Tsvetana Paraskova of OilPrice.com

Smaller oil tankers moved in October the most volumes of crude oil out of the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, as Iran targets supertankers and incidents with naval mines and unknown projectiles hit a wartime high.

The smaller tankers, which can carry less than half the volumes of a supertanker, shipped 2 million barrels per day (bpd) out of the Strait of Hormuz in October, the highest daily volumes since the war began in February, according to Vortexa data cited by Bloomberg.

The shipments on Suezmaxes and Aframaxes, mostly via ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, started to materially pick up in September, which coincided with the estimates that overall crude oil flows via the Strait of Hormuz have rebounded and nearly reached pre-war levels.

Gulf producers and oil importers have had to continuously adapt to the changing security and shipping conditions in and around the Strait of Hormuz. With supertanker rates soaring to record highs in September and early October, and attacks on very large crude carriers (VLCCs) jumping to a wartime high, sellers, traders, shippers, and buyers have started to lean more on the smaller-sized vessels to move crude out of the Persian Gulf.

Suezmaxes and Aframaxes have been mostly used on routes and cargoes from Kuwait, Iraq, and Qatar, traders and shipbrokers told Bloomberg.

Meanwhile, attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have intensified in recent weeks.

For days, Iran has been reporting nearly daily incidents with tankers hitting naval mines in corridors that Iran has designated as “unauthorized” in the Strait of Hormuz.

Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview last week that the Strait of Hormuz navigation would not return to pre-war conditions, ever.

“There are no ‘free waters’ [international waters] there, and the 1982 [UN Convention on the Law of the Sea] does not apply to the strait … The regulations within the Strait of Hormuz are governed by the laws of the two littoral states that border it,” the official told Al Jazeera.

items.title: Waller Wants To "Shock" People: Fed Hawk Reprises 50bps Call As Market Refuses To Price It
items.content_text:
Waller Wants To "Shock" People: Fed Hawk Reprises 50bps Call As Market Refuses To Price It

He's back.

Eight days after threatening a 50bps hike hours before CPI, Fed Governor Chris Waller went on CNBC this morning and did it again: inflation is headed in the wrong direction, it is broadening, and policymakers should consider a half-point increase at the Dec. 9 decision. And just in case anyone thought he was bluffing, he told CNBC's Steve Liesman that "You might need to, like, shock people."

The 2-year yield promptly erased a 2.5bp drop and rose as much as 2.8bp to 4.83%, while the 10Y spiked to a session high of 5.13% before fading back to 5.09%. And yet, with OIS still pricing a full quarter-point hike plus just ~3bps extra, the market puts the odds of Waller getting his way at roughly 10%. Which raises two questions: how far is the market from pricing it, and what happens to the AI bid and a long end already sitting at 5.1% if he does.

70% Of Core Services Above 3%... "Nothing To Do With Oil"

The case Waller laid out was less about the headline and more about breadth. By his count, roughly 70% of the items in the core services basket are now rising by more than 3%, a sign that the inflation impulse has long since escaped the energy shock (so much for "transitory pass-through"). Annualized, he said, inflation is heading toward 3.5%.

What seems to worry him most is pricing power: companies increasingly believe consumers are resilient enough to swallow price increases of 3% or more, and so the Fed may need to "shock" people out of thinking 3% is the new normal. Waller also said the Fed may have to take back all three of last year's "insurance" cuts, and maybe more. Insurance, as it turns out, against the wrong risk.

He did offer an alternative: hike 25bps in December and explicitly signal another move in January. The catch, as CNBC noted, is that this runs against how Chair Warsh likes to communicate (i.e., not pre-committing). Put differently, Waller is telling his boss: either give me 50 now, or give me forward guidance he doesn't want to give. Either way it's 50bps over two meetings.

Deja Waller

Regular readers will recall that the London version of Waller put it like this on Nov 10, at the BoE Watchers conference, conditioning a 50bp move on October core CPI printing around 0.3% or higher:

In that case, I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting. Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take.

Core CPI then printed 0.3% hours later (0.297% unrounded, so the threshold was met by the grace of rounding), odds of a 50bps hike jumped to about 14%, and ZH tweeted the "hawkish panic" in real time. Then the softer PPI trimmed those bets, and as we noted last week, none of Waller's colleagues joined him in openly backing 50.

That hasn't changed. Per Goldman's US economics team (Mericle), the closest thing to a response came from the New York Fed's John Williams, who said Tuesday: "I don't think the situation calls for dramatic action". Williams also argued the October core print reflected a continuation, not a broadening, of tariff and energy passthrough, which is the polar opposite of Waller's "spreading out" diagnosis (and since both vote, someone is going to be disappointed). Meanwhile, St. Louis Fed's Musalem sees several increases by spring.

For those keeping score, this is the same Waller who flipped dovish in early September and sent everything ripping. Ten weeks later he wants to shock the public. Data dependence at its finest.

How Far Is The Market From Pricing It?

Short answer: about 22bps. Waller wants 50; OIS prices ~28bps for Dec. 9 (a done-deal 25bps plus a ~10% chance of the larger move), and Goldman's own forecast is a plain-vanilla 25bps.

The pricing has actually come off the boil: the December contract spiked to roughly 29bps right after CPI and had faded to ~25.8bps by Tuesday's close, per Goldman's Marquee chart (chart source GS FICC). More interesting is what's behind it: another ~17bps is priced for January and ~17bps for March, or roughly 60bps of hikes through the spring (napkin math, assuming the pricing is cumulative per meeting).

Goldman's Mericle reads the October FOMC as a compromise to hike every other meeting, and after last week's CPI the bank added a third 25bp hike in March 2027, after a second one in December (full note available to pro subs). In other words, the street has the destination right and is arguing about the speed, which is exactly what Waller's "25 plus a January signal" option is about.

What 50 Does To The AI Bid And A 5.1% Long End

Here is the awkward timing: Waller's hawkish encore landed just as Nvidia's beat-and-raise was supposed to rescue a battered tech complex ahead of today's must-price Anthropic IPO. Goldman's Rich Privorotsky summed up the Nvidia print: "The spending isn’t stopping". NDX had been re-testing its local lows into the print, per Goldman's Mark Flood, and futures were up ~0.3% this morning before Waller dented the mood, with gold's slide accelerating to below $3,800, the lowest since Sept 2025. 

The problem for the AI trade is that it no longer runs on cash flow. As we have been warning since last October, AI is now a debt bubble too, and a Fed that front-loads hikes raises the cost of every dollar of that debt just as Apollo's CEO talks about an $8 trillion buildout bill. (Waller, for his part, said concerns about AI financing are limited to the banks. Maybe.)

As for the long end, the 10Y was at 5.10% this morning per Goldman's desk, and the plumbing isn't helping: Tuesday's long-end Treasury buyback used only about 20% of announced capacity ($1.18BN accepted), versus the full $6BN in the previous operation. A 50bp hike would likely mean a bear flattener at first, with the front end doing the heavy lifting. Then again, with the 30-year mortgage rate at 7.35% (MBA) and building permits collapsing 7.4%, below every single forecast, a long end at 5.1% is already doing a fair bit of tightening on Waller's behalf.

Minutes At 2pm, Shock In December?

Next up are the FOMC minutes at 2pm, where Goldman will be looking for the assumptions behind participants' outlooks and their views of the balance of risks. Since the October meeting, the inflation and labor data have, on net, come in firmer than expected, so the minutes will probably read stale on arrival.

Our take: Waller probably doesn't get his 50 in December (November CPI lands on Dec. 10, the day after the decision, and Williams isn't there yet). But he very likely gets the next best thing: a December hike paired with a January signal. Which means the real mispricing sits in the ~17bps priced for January, far more than in the 10% odds of 50 for December... along with a long end at 5.1% that hasn't fully done the math yet.

Much more in Goldman's Fed preview note, available to pro subs.

Estimates, rating and price target. Raising FY27 bookings 19% on higher GTA 6 units (now at 65M vs. 35M prior. As a result of higher bookings, our FY27 non-GAAP EPS rises 56% to $9.61 vs. $6.16 prior). While our FY27 estimates move up meaningfully, FY28 remains unchanged (bookings flat, non-GAAP EPS +2% on lower mobile UA spend estimate). We maintain our $300 PT, implies 30x CY29 FCF / sh of $13.15 ($13.43 prior) discounted back to CY26 at 10% / year.

TTWO shares are up 4.5% in premarket trading, but the stock has traded sideways for nearly two years.

Jefferies gaming analyst James Heaney noted earlier this week: "We believe the bigger opportunity is the duration of the GTA VI monetization cycle." Read note here.

items.title: Dutch Startup Boasts Its Missiles Helped Destroy Crimea Bridge, & Is Now In Russia's Crosshairs
items.content_text:
Dutch Startup Boasts Its Missiles Helped Destroy Crimea Bridge, & Is Now In Russia's Crosshairs

The early Tuesday major Ukrainian attack on Crimea's Kerch Strait Bridge was one of the most significant strikes on Russian territory and assets of the recent war, and could prove as a turning point leading to further serious escalation - given Moscow is not going to sit idly by.

As a reminder, President Zelensky was quick to boast about the destruction of the main span of the bridge, which lies in a mangled concrete and steel mess in the Kerch Strait, blocking the ship lane. What's more is that Zelensky in a rarity named the specific weapons systems used - among them a key foreign-made weapon.

"Today, at the key stage, the 'Palianytsia' drones performed exceptionally well, striking the road section of the bridge, while 'Neptune' missiles, 'Ruta’ drones, and FP-5 drones struck the railway section. Using 'Flamingo,' our warriors carried out a precision-guided strike, and the communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds," Zelensky wrote on X.

Soon after, Dutch arms manufacturer Destinus stepped out of the shadows and openly proclaimed its role, stating that seven of its RUTA missiles destroyed part of the crossing.

"We are proud to support the Ukrainian defence forces in their fight to defend Ukraine and Europe," the Hengelo and Valkenburg-based company announced in a LinkedIn post. It marks the first time that Destinus has ever publicly claimed that its weapons were behind attack operations by Ukraine.

"Last night’s strikes damaged the bridge's upper load-bearing structure. Today, seven RUTA missiles hit the bridge, causing one span to collapse," Destinus wrote in the Tuesday post.

The European start-up further revealed that its LORD and Da Vinci unmanned systems "were also deployed to suppress Russian air defences" amid the riskey operation. A spokesperson for the company has also told European outlets, "we felt it was important to show that technology developed in Europe, together with Ukrainian weapons, can make a concrete contribution to the defense of Europe."

Did this effectively just make The Netherlands a target for Russian retaliation or potential sabotage attacks? 

The Russian Embassy in the Netherlands on Wednesday is demanding answers. Destinus could now be in the crosshairs:

According to missile expert Fabian Hoffman, the current announcement just puts Destinus on the map — and not in a good way.

While the publicity from a successful attack can bring new customers, “we know that Russia has gone after these types of companies in Europe,” he tells NOS.

And, arguably, Destinus is on Russia’s radar already. Earlier this year, Russia’s Ministry of Defence named the company on a list of European weapons producers. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, stated that the sites on that list should be seen as legitimate targets.

The Russian Embassy said in a statement on X, "Moscow has been duly informed of the NL (Netherlands) involvement."

"The confession has been well noted. Is The Hague openly joining the conflict?" it questioned.

This episode may go down in history as the first time LinkedIn has played a role in a start-up confessing its involvement in stoking a major regional war, and which portends significant escalation. Most defense firms have been content to provide their weapons covertly and in silence while not poking the Russian bear too loudly, but apparently Destinus - despite it being a young and small company - has come out of the gate swinging. Helping launch WW3 just for some clout?

Tyler Durden Wed, 11/18/2026 - 08:30

items.title: Futures Rise As Huang-less Nvidia Beats And Raises, Gold Crashes Below $3,800
items.content_text:
Futures Rise As Huang-less Nvidia Beats And Raises, Gold Crashes Below $3,800

US futures are higher (but well off highs) as Nvidia's first earnings report without Jensen Huang delivered a clean beat-and-raise that soothed frayed AI nerves, while oil reversed an earlier slide after a surprise build in US crude stockpiles and precious metals have gotten monkeyhammered, with gold tumbling below $3,800 for the first time since September 2025. Sentiment was dented, however, and gold slide accelerated after Fed Governor Waller warned the Fed may need to take more "aggressive" action to bring price pressures down including a 50bps rate hike. As a result 10Y yields reversed an earlier drop to trade near session highs of 5.12% ahead of this afternoon's FOMC minutes. As of 7:00am ET, S&P futures are 0.2% higher at 7,370 while Nasdaq futures gain 0.6% and Dow futures are 0.2% lower; contracts have faded from their overnight highs, when Nasdaq futures were up as much as 2%. That follows a nasty Tuesday session in which the S&P fell 1% and closed below its 200DMA, decliners outnumbered gainers about 6 to 1 and all 11 sectors fell. In premarket trading, the Mag 7 is mostly higher with Nvidia (NVDA) up about 3% and dragging AI infrastructure names like Nebius, CoreWeave, Coherent and Credo up 5-7.5%, as we previewed last night; semis are up 2.8% and memory 3.5%, per JPM. The day's driver is Nvidia (again): the company guided Q4 revenue to $130 billion versus a street at about $125 billion, lifted its FY28 growth outlook to 75% from 70%, added $150 billion to its buyback and excluded China entirely from its numbers, while the board shut the door on Huang's return. Treasuries edge higher with the curve flattening, as gilts lead European bonds after UK October CPI (3.6%) and services inflation came in below the Bank of England's forecasts; the dollar is bid, sending EURUSD to a fresh 19-month low of 1.0965. Oil slides with WTI just above $84 and Brent near $92, gold is down 2.1% at $3,769, silver drops 3.6% and LME copper breaks below $13,000/t. Bitcoin is flat around $64,300. US economic data slate includes MBA mortgage applications (7am), October housing starts and building permits (8:30am), pending home sales (10am), FOMC minutes (2pm) and TIC flows (4pm). Fed speaker slate includes Daly (12:15pm), Barr (1:35pm), Williams (2:30pm) and Kashkari (4:15pm). The Treasury sells $16 billion of 20-year bonds at 1pm.

In premarket trading, Mag 7 stocks are mostly higher: (Nvidia (NVDA) +3%, Alphabet (GOOGL) +1%, Tesla (TSLA) +0.9%, Amazon (AMZN) +0.5%, Microsoft (MSFT) unchanged, Meta Platforms (META) -0.1%, Apple (AAPL) -0.2%)

  • AI infrastructure stocks including Broadcom (AVGO), CoreWeave (CRWV) are rising after Nvidia’s solid sales outlook.
  • Applied Optoelectronics (AAOI) drops 10% after the maker of fiber‑optic networking products said it plans to offer up to $550 million in common stock from time to time under an equity distribution agreement.
  • Bullish (BLSH) gains 8% after the crypto exchange reported third-quarter adjusted Ebitda that beat the average analyst estimate.
  • Dolby Labs (DLB) falls 3% after the developer of audio and voice technologies gave a 2027 forecast for adjusted earnings per share that missed the consensus estimate.
  • Lowe’s (LOW) slips 3% after the home improvement retailer’s third quarter adj. EPS topped expectations by 18c, but management maintained its annual guidance. All together, the implied 4Q adj. EPS $1.72 trails the consensus estimate of $1.98.
  • Sellas Life (SLS) is down 2% after the drug developer announced a $150 million share offering, following the stock’s biggest one-day gain in almost six years on Tuesday.
  • Take-Two Interactive (TTWO) climbs nearly 6% as positive reviews come in for the firm’s Grand Theft Auto VI game, which is set to officially launch on Thursday.
  • Tandem Diabetes (TNDM) gains 4% after Stifel upgraded the medical device maker to buy, citing market expansion and improving margins.

In other corporate news, Anthropic is on the cusp of pricing what may be the biggest IPO of all time, reportedly drawing multiple orders of $10 billion or more and guiding to the top of its $70-78 range or above, while crypto futures tied to the debut imply a valuation of about $1.7 trillion versus $1.4 trillion at the top of the range (nothing frothy to see here). Target raised its full-year adjusted EPS guidance to $10.65-11.40 from $9.90-10.90, and both Target and Lowe's lifted their sales guidance; TJX also reports before the open. Nvidia has stopped selling its licensed Hopper data-center chips to China and former CEO Jensen Huang agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, according to Politico, while Democrats plan a probe of Commerce Secretary Lutnick's and Cantor Fitzgerald's Nvidia ties. Citigroup and JPMorgan added language to financing documents for a potential loan making the borrower responsible for complying with chip-access restrictions. Medline backers including Blackstone and Carlyle raised $2.1 billion in a share sale priced at $35.50, Applied Optoelectronics slides 11% after unveiling a $550 million at-the-market stock offering, and Tencent's Q3 revenue of 207.3 billion yuan missed estimates as AI spending squeezed profit.

Investors woke up to relief rather than euphoria: Bloomberg's Neil Campling notes that some had feared Nvidia would withdraw guidance altogether, so the higher FY28 target was a pleasant surprise, and the price action today will tell us whether AI momentum can rebound or whether this is merely a short-covering pop from oversold levels. Bulls can point to the raised guide, the demand commentary and capital return; bears to softer gross margins, rising DSOs, ballooning balance sheet commitments and the unresolved CEO succession. Perhaps the most important tell came from interim CEO Colette Kress, who described future ecosystem investments as "disciplined" and "rigorous", suggesting the "bank of Nvidia" backstop for the AI buildout will be dialed back, confirming our article on the $320 billion of AI project finance that needs a guarantor. Which begs the question of who funds the next leg when Apollo's CEO says the AI buildout could demand as much as $8 trillion of financing.

Commenting on the overnight action, Marija Veitmane at State Street Global Markets told Bloomberg that “Nvidia earnings and guidance confirmed what we have heard from all other technology companies: AI capex is strong and shows little sign of a slowdown. Strong earnings coupled with lower valuation and positioning make the sector an attractive opportunity.” 

How Nvidia and CoreWeave trade on Thursday will offer a strong signal on the road ahead for the tech trade, according to Tom Essaye at The Sevens Report. “If those stocks open higher and extend the gains throughout the day, that’s a signal that perhaps the tech correction may be ending,” Essaye noted. “However, if both pop at the open but finish the day negative, that tells us investors are using strength to reduce AI infrastructure positions.”

The relief comes after a brutal stretch for the chipmaker, which had reached its most oversold level since 2019 going into the print, and after fund managers dumped tech at the fastest pace since 2006. Bloomberg's Equity Insights adds that the S&P has until Dec. 3 to complete a pattern that delivered gains after three of the past four major volatility shocks: the front of the VIX futures curve inverted by 2.34 points on Nov. 5, a level of backwardation that has preceded a higher index four weeks later in most episodes since 2016.

The flip side is the Fed. Bloomberg Economics chief US economist Anna Wong highlights that volatility shocks are driving Treasury yields higher, and estimates that a theoretical AI crash early next year would cut 2027 GDP growth by 1.5 percentage points from a baseline of around 2%, while blowing out the fiscal deficit. Her key point: long-dated Treasuries have become a less reliable hedge against equity selloffs after a flip in the relationship between yields and the VIX.

OCBC FX strategist Moh Siong Sim says Fed hawks are keeping further tightening in play, which should keep the dollar supported, with the FOMC minutes the next key test of the Fed's hawkish shift. With futures fully pricing a 25bp December hike, the minutes matter less for the decision itself than for how broad support is for further tightening, and whether officials worry that AI investment is keeping aggregate demand hotter than expected. NY Fed President Williams overnight said the Fed still has work to do on inflation but dismissed the need for an outsized hike.

Over at Goldman, Rich Privorotsky says Nvidia "did pretty much everything you could ask for": a beat and raise, a $130 billion guide versus roughly $125 billion expected and zero China data-center compute baked in, in short the spending isn't stopping; the only thing missing was a hint Jensen could come back, and that was shut down. He notes the tape "felt different" on Tuesday, with high-beta momentum up, AI outperforming the AI losers and expensive defensives that had gone too far finally catching down, which he found somewhat constructive from a gross standpoint. Privorotsky admits his "contrarian muscles are starting to flex a little on AI": he understands haircutting 2028 and fretting about a 2029 peak, but given the dollars still to be spent, how far multiples have compressed (SK Hynix trades at 1.79x blended 24-month P/E) and what investors are paying for defensives, some of these names could go up quickly. On cyber, he thinks much of the anxiety stemmed from the assumption that the outages were connected, and sees anxiety on the topic at local highs, noting that Costco sold out of 21 of its 26 high-ticket generator models online by Sunday. Technically, he says the velocity of CTA selling may have peaked but the magnitude can still be considerable, especially in Europe, with the S&P "hanging on to the 200d by a fingernail."

Privorotsky's bigger macro point is about commodities: copper, crude, gasoline, diesel and parts of the grain complex are all falling, and if that sticks it is "a meaningful disinflationary impulse"; his trade is long front-end bonds alongside equities. He also notes that gold still can't hold a bounce even with relief in yields, suggesting there may be a liquidation element, while the China tape has been "objectively awful", perhaps a sign that policy is way too tight.

JPM's Market Intel desk under Andrew Tyler remains Tactically Bullish, arguing Nvidia's print helps the market climb the latest wall of worry, but it may take a few more days to coax buyers off the sidelines because Nvidia's long-term outlook was not resolved and investors may use up-days to keep cutting positions. The desk also flags a bullish October retail sales print, with the control group up 0.6% versus 0.3% expected, as evidence the consumer remains the anchor of the economy, though it may add to Fed hawkishness. JPM's Ed Bell, back from the bank's APAC tech conference, says he can't recall a bigger gap between upbeat corporate commentary and universally negative investor feedback.

Goldman's TMT desk (Sean Johnstone) notes Nvidia's total commitments jumped to $518 billion from $366 billion, including $74 billion of data center leases, and flags that Kress dialing back the "bank of AI" role is positive for Nvidia credit but negative for leveraged neoclouds, even as Nebius and CoreWeave jumped 10% after hours; software got hit again on the "AI agents replace seats" thesis, with Salesforce down 9% on Tuesday. GS Prime data show fundamental long/short net leverage fell to its lowest in more than five years, below the Liberation Day lows, with the six-week pace of Info Tech selling the fastest in a decade, which the team says sets up a possible tactical rally. Meanwhile, derivatives strategist Gail Hafif expects Nvidia earnings and today's VIX expiry to take significant vol premium out of the market as dealer short tails roll off, as we discussed earlier this week.

Sentiment was dented this morning after Fed Governor Chris Waller told CNBC on Wednesday he was "very concerned" that inflation was moving in the wrong direction and becoming more broad-based, warning the US central bank may need to take more "aggressive" action to bring price pressures down. Waller said roughly 70% of items in the core services basket were rising by more than 3%, a sign that inflationary pressure was not simply related to oil. He also expressed concern that companies increasingly believed consumers were resilient enough to absorb price increases of 3% or more. The Fed may need to "shock" people out of thinking that 3% inflation is an acceptable norm, Waller said.

In geopolitics, Trump touched down in Shenzhen, where Xi met him in person at the airport in a rare gesture; the APEC summit runs through Nov. 19 and the Kremlin says Putin and Trump will meet several times (here is what analysts expect). In the Gulf, the US struck Qeshm Island and Iran targeted a US base in Kuwait, while an ADNOC vessel was attacked transiting Hormuz; yet oil keeps falling as supply glut worries dominate.

Pepperstone strategist Dilin Wu wrote that “The next test of risk appetite in the AI sector will be Anthropic’s IPO. If shares continue to attract steady buying interest at elevated valuations, it could support risk appetite across the broader AI sector.” Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM Trade, was more skeptical: “The bigger question remains unanswered. Without Huang as the visible frontman and aggressive dealmaker, the longer-term shape of the company is still opaque.”

In Europe, the Stoxx 600 is steady, up 0.1% at 651.13 after its worst day since March, with 338 members up and 243 down. Tech and industrials lead as chipmakers ASML, ASM International and BE Semiconductor rise after Nvidia, while miners and energy lag as copper and gold slide. JPM's desk says the tech boost is welcome but its trading flows skew to net selling, while Privorotsky warns CTA supply could still be considerable in Europe. Hays soared as much as 29% on a profit outlook well ahead of expectations, while Alstom plunged as much as 9.6% to a 22-year low as analysts speculated about an equity raise. In politics, a new poll shows Le Pen and Mélenchon would beat their rivals in a presidential vote, and Germany nominated Markus Brunnermeier for the ECB chief economist seat, paving the way for Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Lagarde. Here are the biggest European movers:

  • Europe chip stocks edge higher after Nvidia raised its revenue growth outlook for the next fiscal year, a sign of strong demand despite concerns around stricter export regulations and slowing growth at frontier AI labs.
  • Convatec shares rise as much as 10% after the UK medical equipment maker has raised its full-year organic growth guidance.
  • Hays shares rally as much as 29% after the recruitment company said it expects to deliver adjusted operating profit of at least £35 million in the first half, which analysts at Citi said is well ahead of expectations.
  • Alstom shares fall as much as 9.6% to their lowest in 22 years after the French train manufacturer’s results led analysts to speculate on how and when the company will tackle its debt.
  • European mining stocks are leading losses on the Stoxx Europe 600 Index as copper and gold prices decline, with metals pressured by a stronger dollar, AI upheaval and shifting expectations for US rates.
  • Deutz shares fall as much as 16% after Ningi Research published a report on the German engine manufacturer and said it holds a short position.
  • Marshalls drops as much as 8.9% after the UK maker of paving and roofing reported falling sales in its building products division. Management also pointed to a further slowing in new housebuilding activity since the first half of the year.
  • Genus shares slide as much as 5.9% after the animal genetics company warned the depreciation of the Brazilian real and Mexican peso will hit profits this year.
  • Accor shares drop as much as 6.5% after the French hotelier said it has agreed to boost its stake in Ennismore through staged transactions totaling about €1.6 billion. Barclays said the deal “seems expensive.”
  • Carl Zeiss Meditec fell as much as 3.1% after the healthcare systems company’s shares were downgraded by Barclays, which cited a tough operating environment.

Asian stocks were choppy as an early Nvidia bounce faded, leaving the MSCI Asia Pacific Index little changed. Korea's Kospi trimmed an early 3.3% surge but still closed up 2% at 5,067, holding the lows of the prior selloff, which Goldman's Privorotsky calls encouraging; SK Hynix and Samsung gained, and K-content stocks soared after Xi and South Korea's Lee met. Japan's Nikkei rose 0.3% to 59,024, while Taiwan's Taiex swung between gains and losses. Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.9%, pressured by biotech and JD.com after its profit miss, and Tencent missed revenue estimates; the CSI 300 added 0.2% as APEC kicked off in Shenzhen and the PBOC set its strongest yuan fixing since 2022. Australia's ASX fell 0.7% on weakness in tech and gold miners. Indonesia's central bank surprised with a 25bp hike to 6% to defend the rupiah.

In FX, the Bloomberg Dollar Spot Index is up 0.2% and the DXY trades near 103.76, near the top of a 103.58-103.85 range, as traders await the FOMC minutes. EURUSD slides 0.3% to 1.0965, a fresh 19-month low, despite euro-area core inflation being revised up to 2.6%. The pound is the G10 laggard, down 0.4% at 1.3162, after UK CPI undershot and traders trimmed bets on Bank of England hikes, with markets now seeing about an 80% chance of a December move versus 90% before the release. The yen is steady at 159.25, supported by lower energy prices. In EM, the South African rand leads losses as gold drops, and the forint weakens on rate-cut bets.

In rates, Treasuries edge higher for a third day with the curve flattening; the 10Y yield is down about 1bp at 5.09% and the 2Y at 4.79%. Gilts outperform after UK CPI rose 3.6% and services inflation held at 3.7%, both below the BOE's forecasts, sending the UK 10Y down 6bps to 5.31%, even as the BOE unusually put out a statement warning that inflation will rise further into 2027. Bunds also gain as lower crude and Dutch gas prices provide relief, while Germany's 7-year Bund auction drew a 1.5x bid-to-cover. On deck: $75 billion of 17-week bills at 11:30am and $16 billion of 20-year bonds at 1pm, followed by FOMC minutes at 2pm, with a December hike fully priced in. Goldman's Privorotsky likes owning front-end bonds alongside equities here, while Bloomberg's Anna Wong reminds us that the long end, increasingly, hedges nothing.

In commodities, WTI is down 1.9% at $84.39, trading in an $82.38-84.77 range and slipping below its 100DMA, while Brent drops about 1% to $92, after API data showed a surprise 5.3 million barrel crude build (versus an expected draw) and a 5.1 million barrel gasoline build. Geopolitics is being shrugged off: Iran reportedly floated a two-day peace plan that would reopen Hormuz once the US lifts oil sanctions and its naval blockade, Iraq restarted the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline after 12 years, and smaller tankers are keeping Hormuz flows going. Goldman's Privorotsky notes the US 3-2-1 crack spread has collapsed 36% in six weeks to $41.90/bbl, which is why gas is now below $4. Precious metals are in freefall: spot gold dropped as low as $3,757.51 and is on pace for its worst year since 2013, silver is down 3.6% at $45.72, and LME copper slumped to fresh multi-month lows near $12,705/t, with the Bloomberg Commodity Index down 1.6%.

US economic data slate includes MBA mortgage applications (7am), October housing starts and building permits (8:30am), pending home sales (10am), FOMC minutes (2pm) and September TIC flows (4pm). Fed speaker slate includes Daly (12:15pm), Barr (1:35pm), Williams (2:30pm) and Kashkari (4:15pm). Target, Lowe's and TJX report before the open, Palo Alto Networks after the close, and Rockwell Automation and Expeditors host investor days.

Market Snapshot

Top Overnight News

  • Russia imported record volumes of petrol by sea last month, as Ukrainian drone strikes badly damaged refineries and cut the country’s production capacity. Seaborne imports reached 390,000 tons in October, according to data from Kpler, marking a striking reversal in Russia’s traditional role as a fuel exporter and highlighting its vulnerability to Ukrainian attacks on fuel infrastructure: FT
  • After nearly nine months of war, the United States and Iran are each acting as if they have time on their side, a calculation that has locked them in a stalemate that is almost impossible for either to break. It is a risky gamble, with two former US Middle East negotiators, European officials and Gulf sources saying fighting could resume before a diplomatic exit becomes possible: RTRS
  • Iran launched strikes against Kuwait and Bahrain early Wednesday, expanding its targets while continuing attacks against ships trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz: WSJ
  • Banks that have lent billions of dollars to finance the AI infrastructure boom are seeking to rein in their risk exposure, which has come under increasing scrutiny following Democrats’ sweep of the US midterm elections: FT
  • Canadian PM Mark Carney said he’ll meet Trump later today on the sidelines of the APEC summit. He said there’s been some progress on a trade deal, though it was “two steps forward, one step back.”: BBG
  • Singapore expects some impact on the flow of high-end chips through the city-state due to tighter US curbs, though officials said the fallout can be managed: BBG
  • Wall Street banks expect global corporate profit growth to slow sharply next year, as the rapid acceleration in AI investment that has powered an equity bull market begins to ease: FT
  • Overall Book and Fundamental L/S Gross and Net leverage ratios have all declined MTD. Fundamental L/S Gross leverage has fallen -4.4 pts in November MTD to 206.3% (23rd percentile 1-year, 65th percentile 3-year), while Fundamental L/S Net leverage has fallen -7.6 pts MTD to 41.6% (5-year low): GSPB
  • Indonesia’s central bank hiked its main policy rate by 25bp to 6%: Nikkei
  • Xi Jinping greeted Donald Trump at the airport in Shenzhen in a rare move as the US president arrived in China for the APEC summit and talks with Xi and Vladimir Putin. Xi earlier warned against economic barriers, while Putin said sanctions, tariffs and export restrictions couldn’t hold back rising competitors: BBG
  • UK inflation accelerated to its highest level in a year after a surge in energy bills and motor fuel costs. Consumer prices rose 3.6% from a year earlier, up from 3.5% in September and marking a fourth consecutive increase, the Office for National Statistics said on Wednesday. It was in line with economists’ expectations: BBG
  • Japan’s imports were a bit below plan for Oct (+21.6% vs. the Street +25.9%) while exports were about inline (+20.5% vs. the Street +20.4%): BBG
  • Former Nvidia (NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, according to Politico: Politico

A more detailed look at global markets courtesy of Newsquawk

APAC stocks were mixed, with price action choppy throughout the session as the negative lead from Wall Street was partially offset by tailwinds from Nvidia's earnings beat. ASX 200 declined with the index dragged lower by underperformance in tech and gold miners, while nearly all sectors were in the red aside from energy and utilities. Nikkei 225 swung between gains and losses to trade on both sides of the 59,000 level, while the somewhat mixed trade data from Japan did little to shake off the indecisive mood. KOSPI briefly wiped out its initial gains and returned to flat territory as the early boost post-Nvidia earnings petered out, before ultimately catching a second wind. Hang Seng and Shanghai Comp traded mixed, with the Hong Kong benchmark pressured by weakness in biotech stocks and underperformance in JD.com after its Q3 net profit missed expectations, while the mainland ultimately kept afloat as the APEC summit in Shenzhen kicked off.

Top Asian News

  • Chinese President Xi said at the APEC opening ceremony in Shenzhen that global turmoil is deepening and world growth lacks momentum, while he urged APEC members to resolve disputes through discussion and address shared challenges through greater cooperation and unity. Xi said members must firmly uphold the WTO and support free and open trade, and noted that they should expand avenues for mutual benefit and win-win outcomes.
  • Chinese President Xi said in a meeting with South Korean President Lee that China is ready to maintain the stability and smooth operation of global industrial supply chains with South Korea, while Lee said he hopes the two countries will further develop an equal and mutually beneficial economic partnership. Furthermore, Lee said he hopes they can work together to create an era of peaceful coexistence on the Korean Peninsula, and stated that peace and stability are essential to the mature development of their strategic cooperative partnership.
  • Tencent (0700 HK) - Q3 2026 (CNY): Revenue 207.34bln (exp. 210.53bln), Operating Profit 59.2bln (exp. 66.6bln), Adj. Net Profit 66.5bln (exp. 66.5bln). International gaming revenue 18.9bln (exp. 20.4bln, prev. 18.8bln Y/Y), Domestic gaming revenue 47.6bln (exp. 48.0bln, prev. 40.4bln Y/Y), Weixin/WeChat MAUs 1.45bln (exp. 1.43bln, prev. 1.39bln Y/Y), Fee-based VAS subscriptions 253mln (exp. 264mln).
  • Japan's Defence Ministry reportedly informed major defence contractors that spending from the next fiscal year onwards will be sharply lower than previously expected, Kyodo reported.

European bourses (Stoxx 600 +0.1%) are mixed, with the Euro Stoxx 50 the slight outperformer given its large exposure to tech. Surprisingly, the AEX is modestly lower, despite ASML printing gains of over 3%, following Nvidia’s earnings. To recap, Q3 earnings and revenue topped expectations, with data centre sales more than doubling in Q3. In terms of guidance, Q4 revenue is seen at USD 130bln, +/- 3% (exp. USD 125.3bln) while raising its fiscal year 2028 growth forecast to 75% from 70%. Furthermore, an additional USD 150bln of share buybacks was announced. After-hours, shares rose as much as 5%, and are currently +3% pre-market. Returning to Europe, sectors opened with a negative bias but are now mixed. Tech tops the sector pile, with Real Estate and Health Care closely behind. On the other hand, Basic Resources continue to get hit, with 3M LME copper lower by around 4% while spot gold prints losses of around 2% and is back below the USD 3,800/oz handle. US equity futures are firmer across the board, with the NQ outperforming. In terms of technicals, the ES failed to break the recent low of 7322.25 and currently holds around the VWAP of 7410 and above the key support level of 7362. With Nvidia out of the way, focus now turns to the Anthropic IPO, with pricing expected later today. Recent reporting suggests that Anthropic is guiding that it will price at the top end of, or above, its USD 70-78 range. Nvidia (NVDA) - Q3 FY27 (USD): Adj. EPS 2.68 (exp. 2.48), Revenue 115.8bln (exp. 109bln), Data Centre revenue 107.6bln (exp. 101.87bln). Q4 outlook: Revenue 130bln (exp. 125.3bln), Adj. operating expenses about 10.7bln (exp. 9.99bln). Guides fiscal year 2028 revenue growth of 75% (prev. 70%). Announces a USD 150bln increase to its share buyback programme. Click for the session's European pre-market equity newsflow Click for the additional news

Top European News

  • ECB Financial Stability Review (Nov): "The euro area economy has proved resilient so far this year, in the face of energy supply disruptions, trade frictions and extreme weather events."
  • The EU and UK will commit to closer defence industrial cooperation at the summit on November 20th, Politico reported citing a draft statement, with pledges being made on steel, migration and other points.
  • UK PM Burnham has hinted at a reversal of the national insurance hike that former Chancellor Reeves implemented in order to assist hospitality firms in hiring NEETS, LBC reported.
  • Germany is to temporarily cut electricity tax to the EU minimum level in 2027, with a permanent reduction planned, according to the government.

FX

  • Snapshot: G10s are mostly lower against the USD. The JPY holds afloat, benefiting from cooling energy prices, and continues its recent strength. The GBP underperforms in the aftermath of an in-line/cooler-than-expected inflation report.
  • DXY currently holds towards the upper end of a 103.58 to 103.85 range, continuing to build on the strength seen over the past week or so. Nvidia’s strong results will be helping the USD move a little higher, and the looming Anthropic IPO will also be a factor.
  • Attention remains on the geopolitical situation, with crude benchmarks continuing to reside near lows. Retaliation strikes between the US and Iran (US hit Qeshm Island & Iran hit Kuwait/Bahrain), and reports that Iran had hardened its negotiating position since the midterms, have seemingly been outweighed by the risks of a supply glut and the surprise build in crude stockpiles.
  • Given the energy dynamics, yields are lower across the curve. Any bounce back in oil prices will no doubt spark another leg higher in yields, which could see the EUR be pressured even further. Some analysts have touted a potential move towards the 1.08 mark (currently 1.0975).
  • GBP is the underperformer today, following the UK’s in-line/cooler-than-expected CPI report. In brief, headline Y/Y ticked a little higher to 3.6%, but fell short of the expected 3.7%; headline M/M matched the consensus. The closely watched core components printed in-line, whilst services Y/Y remained steady vs expectations of a tick higher. Following the report, Cable fell from 1.3193 to 1.3172 within 10 minutes, and continued to extend lower to make a session trough of 1.3148.
  • Money markets now assign an 80% chance of a hike in December (vs 90% pre-release). Whilst the report does reduce the odds of near-term tightening, headline metrics remain elevated and will keep the discussion very much open between December and February. If oil prices continue to head lower, market pricing will increasingly shift more dovish; as it stands, SONIA futures imply c. 90bps of further tightening by September, which MUFG believes is “excessive”.

Central Banks

  • BoJ Governor Ueda said the BoJ will continue raising interest rates in line with economic, inflation and financial developments, with financial conditions remaining accommodative. He stressed the importance of underlying inflation becoming firmly anchored at 2%, while noting food consumption tax cuts are likely to have a limited impact. Ueda warned a weaker yen could raise food prices through higher import costs and that long-term yields could rise if BoJ bond purchases are perceived as financing fiscal policy.
  • BoE said it will continue setting interest rates to ensure inflation returns sustainably to the 2% target and expects inflation to rise further by mid-2027 due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.
  • ECB's Vujcic said the ECB discussed opening its balance sheet to funds but decided against it, although the proposal could return. He added that hedge fund activity was partly responsible for rapid increases in spreads earlier this year.

Fixed Income

  • Gilts outperform after a cool set of UK CPI data, Bunds also bid though to a lesser extent while USTs are flat.
  • Gilts eclipsed 85.00 to an 85.34 peak, firmer by over 70 ticks on the day. The morning’s October CPI series came in cooler than the market and BoE expected for the headline and services Y/Y prints, while the core was shy of the BoE’s view, but as the market forecast. A reading that removes some of the impetus behind a back-to-back hike in December, hence the outperformance in Gilts. However, the BoE then unusually provided a statement reiterating that it expects inflation to rise in 2027 amid pressures already in the pipeline. Note, the BoE commenting on the inflation series appears to be the setting of a precedent for upcoming prints.
  • A statement that, logically, can only really be to keep the market from unwinding expectations around a December hike too much. Nonetheless, we do get the November print the day before the December meeting, which will now potentially be crucial in terms of pricing into that decision. Further, and also somewhat offsetting the dovish move seen this morning, Cornwall Insights provided its final forecast ahead of the Ofgem January-March 2027 update, and it expects a 26% increase to household bills. An increase that will mark a significant price move, but on the flip side, will also likely weigh significantly on household activity.
  • Bunds are bid by 24 ticks, just off a 122.22 peak for the day. The European docket is light. Focus on the energy moves, with crude lower and Dutch TTF notably so, and providing some relief to the benchmark with yields retreating a touch. Elsewhere, focus remains on the upcoming ECB appointments, as Politico reported that Germany is set to get the Chief Economist role that Lane is vacating, a point which would then logically set it up for a de Cos presidency, in order to avoid two relatively hawkish members (i.e. a Knot presidency) in two of the key spots.
  • USTs essentially flat, in narrow 105-12 to 105-23+ confines. Performance that comes ahead of numerous Fed officials, and as the US market digests Nvidia earnings and awaits the Anthropic IPO.
  • Germany sells EUR 2.272bln vs exp. EUR 3bln 3.30% 2033 Bund: b/c 1.5x (prev. 1.4x), average yield 3.27% (prev. 3.36%), retention 24.27%.
  • Japan sells JPY 525.8bln 20yr JGB; b/c 3.64x (prev. 5.84x), average yield 3.756% (prev. 3.7230%), Tail in price 0.29 (prev. 0.07).

Commodities

  • Crude benchmarks are lower, extending overnight declines after the latest private sector inventory data showed a surprise build in headline crude stockpiles (Crude +5.3mln vs exp. -0.5mln; Gasoline +5.1mln vs exp. +1.6mln), adding to recent supply glut woes. In geopolitics, Al-Akhbar reported details of Iran's two-day peace proposal, which requires the US to end hostilities, lift oil sanctions and its naval blockade, and release frozen Iranian assets before Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz. This comes after sources said US-Qatar discussions on Iran have been "extremely positive", and despite Iran's attack on Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base, which seems more targeted than widespread. Attention also turns to US President Trump's arrival in China ahead of the historic US-China-Russia trilateral meeting, although no major breakthroughs are expected, while Kremlin aide Ushakov said Putin and Trump could hold several conversations during the APEC summit.
  • WTI Jan'27 trades within a USD 82.38-84.77/bbl range (vs yesterday's USD 83.41-85.97/bbl range), slipping beneath its 100 DMA at USD 83.38/bbl, while Brent Jan'27 moves within USD 91.00-93.37/bbl (vs yesterday's USD 91.26-94.18/bbl range). Dutch TTF is lower within a EUR 81.77-86.49/MWh range (vs yesterday's EUR 83.75-86.92/MWh range), potentially tracking the weakness in crude.
  • Spot gold is lower within a USD 3,757.51-3,857.48/oz range (vs yesterday's USD 3,836.96-3,891.08/oz range), falling beneath the USD 3,800/oz level as the Dollar firms and rate hike expectations weigh, leaving the yellow metal well beneath its 21 DMA at USD 3,986/oz. Spot silver underperforms within a USD 45.60-47.62/oz range (vs yesterday's USD 46.84-48.01/oz range), while platinum and palladium are also sharply lower.
  • 3M LME copper slumps within a USD 12,705.10-13,299.48/t range, breaking beneath the USD 13,000/t level to fresh multi-month lows, pressured by the firmer Dollar and potentially lingering concerns over AI-related demand as tech names struggle. Base metals are broadly lower, with aluminium, nickel and zinc all in the red.
  • US Private Energy Inventory Data (bbls) Crude +5.3mln (exp. -0.5mln), Gasoline +5.1mln (exp. +1.6mln), Distillate +0.4mln (exp. +1.1mln), Cushing -1.7mln
  • EU Council announced a provisional deal with the EU Parliament to speed up permits for renewable energy, electricity grids and storage projects.
  • Russia's Novatek said that it has signed a contract to supply LNG to Turkey and will redirect European energy supplies to China, Interfax reported.

Trade/Tariffs

  • US President Trump said he consummated a big trade deal with the Philippines and that it is a magnificent deal for both sides, while he added that the trade deal took place very quickly and they didn't know it was going to take place.
  • Canadian PM Carney said Canada and the US are making progress on trade negotiations and is scheduled to meet US President Trump later today.
  • Canada's Foreign Minister said resolving trade tensions with China is exceptionally important, pledging progress on trade, investment, energy and national protection, while it was also stated that the priority is North American auto supply chains and limiting Chinese EV presence.
  • UK PM Burnham is to sign a deal this week that would tie the UK to the bloc's agrifood rules and would force the UK to abandon its vow to ban foie gras imports, according to FT.

Geopolitics: Middle East

  • Iran has reportedly proposed a two-day peace plan requiring Washington to end hostilities, lift oil sanctions and its naval blockade, and release frozen Iranian assets on the first day, before Tehran reopens the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping and begins negotiations on a final agreement, including its nuclear programme, on the second day. The main sticking point remains the sequencing of commitments, with the US reportedly seeking nuclear concessions upfront and deferring some obligations, while Qatari mediation has yet to resolve the impasse, according to Al-Akhbar citing a diplomatic source.
  • US and Western officials said Iran is seen to have hardened its negotiating position since the midterms and is emboldened by the GOP losses, according to NYT.
  • Several US soldiers were reportedly injured in a drone attack on Sheikh Isa Air Base in Bahrain, according to Iranian state media citing unnamed sources.
  • ADNOC L&S confirmed one of its vessels was attacked while transiting the Strait of Hormuz on the evening of November 17th 2026.
  • Kuwait's air defences responded to hostile drone attacks, while Arab sources reported explosions heard in Kuwait and southern Iraq near the border. Iran's army later said it targeted US Patriot air-defence systems and launch platforms at the Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait.
  • Bahrain sounded air raid sirens and warned of possible danger, while explosions were reportedly heard.

Geopolitics: Ukraine

  • Russia hit infrastructure facilities in Ukraine's Port of Izmail and a cargo vessel bound for the Pivdennyi port.
  • Two industrial facilities in Russia's Krasnodar region caught fire after a drone attack.

Crypto

  • Bitcoin continues to consolidate following last week's selloff, with the crypto holding in a narrow USD 64.07k-64.93k range.

US Event Calendar

  • 7:00am: Nov 13 MBA Mortgage Applications, prior 6.2%
  • 8:30am: Oct Housing Starts, est. 1250k, prior 1221k
  • 8:30am: Oct Housing Starts MoM, est. 2.4%, prior -5.2%
  • 8:30am: Oct P Building Permits, est. 1375k, prior 1398k
  • 10:00am: Oct Pending Home Sales MoM, est. -2.0%, prior -7.3%
  • 10:00am: Oct Pending Home Sales NSA YoY, est. -14.5%, prior -12.6%

  • 1:00pm: US to sell $16bn 20-year bonds
  • 2:00pm: FOMC Meeting Minutes (Oct. 28 meeting)

Central Bank Speakers
